extracted.intended_audience: general public, researchers, and policymakers interested in genomics and patent law
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating whether genetic material (e.g., isolated genes, cDNA) and related biotechnology inventions qualify as patentable subject matter under U.S. law, with reference to the Myriad Supreme Court decision and its policy implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of a patent (right conferred)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent is granted by individual countries and gives an inventor the legal right to exclude others from making, using, selling, or importing their invention without permission of the patent holder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This describes the function and territorial exclusivity of patent rights and why entities pursue patents (monopoly on use/exploitation). Useful when assessing incentives, enforcement scope, and economic effects of patenting biological discoveries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable subject matter general rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentable subject matter must be concrete, rather than an abstract idea, and laws of nature, products of nature, and natural phenomena are not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the baseline legal standard for subject-matter eligibility: focus on whether the claimed subject is a human-made concrete invention versus an ineligible natural law/product/phenomenon. Apply when analyzing biotech claims to determine whether they cross the statutory/constitutional boundary for patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolated human genes are not patentable (Myriad holding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Isolated human genes were not patentable because the location and order of nucleotides in gene sequences are dictated by nature, not human intervention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a controlling precedent for claims that merely isolate genomic DNA sequences without sufficient human alteration: if the claimed invention is essentially the same sequence/order found in nature, it is likely ineligible under Myriad.

rubrics_metrics.name: cDNA can be patentable (human alteration doctrine)
rubrics_metrics.description: Complementary DNA, cDNA, was determined to be patentable material because humans alter the gene by removing introns—non-coding regions of DNA—from the DNA sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish claims to cDNA (which reflect human-directed modification of natural sequences) from claims to native genomic DNA. The presence of meaningful human alteration may support subject-matter eligibility; analyze the nature and extent of the alteration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolation-and-purification historical precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: Historic logic held that isolating and purifying a gene sequence from surrounding genetic material differentiates the isolated gene from its natural occurrence in the genome (e.g., first whole-gene patent awarded to Genentech in 1982).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This doctrine was used to justify patents on isolated natural products; post-Myriad, its applicability is limited. When reviewing older patents or filings, note that earlier approvals relied on isolation/purification reasoning that courts later questioned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic/utility rationale for patenting genes
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents gave companies like Myriad exclusive rights to cancer screening and genetic testing, creating effective monopolies and large commercial returns (e.g., Myriad made more than $2.5 billion between 1998 and 2013).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the economic impact and utility of gene patents: patents can incentivize investment and development of diagnostics/therapies, but they also confer monopolies that affect access, pricing, and follow-on research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy trade-off: incentives versus impediments to research
rubrics_metrics.description: There were generally two sides: one says patenting human genes will impede new advances in biotechnology and threaten research; the other says without patents no one will do research in this area or develop needed tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as an evaluative dimension when assessing whether patent protection is socially optimal in biotech: weigh potential impediments to research and access against incentives for innovation and investment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of case impact given technological change
rubrics_metrics.description: The Myriad decision ended up having little impact on biotechnology research because technology (e.g., high-throughput sequencing, CRISPR-era tools) has outclassed single-gene, semi-automated sequencing approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging the practical effect of judicial or policy changes on biotechnology, account for contemporaneous and subsequent technological developments that may mitigate or amplify legal rulings' real-world consequences.
